The Hatch-Waxman Act, also known as the Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act, was enacted in 1984 to encourage the development of generic drugs by providing incentives for pharmaceutical companies to file abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

Under the Hatch-Waxman Act, a generic drug manufacturer can file an ANDA seeking approval to market a generic version of a brand-name drug once the patent on the brand-name drug has expired or been invalidated. The FDA then reviews the ANDA and grants approval if it determines that the generic drug is bioequivalent to the brand-name drug.

However, the Hatch-Waxman Act also provides for a period of exclusivity for the brand-name drug manufacturer during which time generic drug manufacturers cannot file ANDAs seeking approval to market a generic version of the brand-name drug. This exclusivity period is intended to provide an incentive for pharmaceutical companies to invest in research and development of new drugs, as they can recoup their investment costs before facing competition from generic drug manufacturers.

Recent U.S. court rulings have expanded the scope of patent exclusivity periods under the Hatch-Waxman Act. For example, in 2013, the Supreme Court ruled in Sandoz Inc. v. Amgen Inc. that a generic drug manufacturer could not challenge the validity of a brand-name drug's patent during the period of exclusivity granted to the brand-name drug manufacturer under the Hatch-Waxman Act. In addition, recent court rulings have clarified that the exclusivity period granted to a brand-name drug manufacturer under the Hatch-Waxman Act applies not only to the brand-name drug itself but also to any patented methods of using the drug.
